title: WTT's money, part two: where it comes from, and what the 2025 accounts show
seo_title: WTT's money part two: the 2025 loss and the 15%
description: The ITTF made a surplus in 2024 and a $14.4m loss in 2025. What the accounts show about WTT's money, its 15% shareholder and the US Smash. Part two.
standfirst: WTT made its first profit in 2024 and the wider ITTF group then lost $14.4m in 2025. The published accounts show where the costs have grown, why the revenue mix has changed and why a 15% shareholding has never been fully explained.
body: This is part two of two. Part one, [WTT's money, part one: China's money, and where it actually goes](/news/wtt-china-money-table-tennis-part-one), looks at what China contributes to WTT and why tournament money there does not automatically reach it.

In 2024 the ITTF made money. In 2025 it lost $14.4m. Those two figures, from the group's consolidated accounts, frame the question of how professional table tennis pays for itself, and they are the sharpest numbers the sport has published about its own business.

WTT is part of that group. The ITTF's statement on its 2023 and 2024 accounts says WTT recorded its first profit in 2024, contributing to a group surplus of US$1.5m. The 2025 accounts show a group net deficit of US$14.4m. Those accounts cover the whole group, not WTT alone, and WTT does not publish standalone figures, so the business that runs the events cannot be separated from the federation that owns it.
## Where the money comes from
The published record and press reports point to four main sources of income for WTT and its group.

- Commercial rights. Sponsorship, media and streaming rights, hosting rights, and betting and data rights. Since 2020 IMG has handled WTT's media rights, production, sponsorship sales and betting data.
- Event income. Ticket sales, hospitality, merchandise and local sponsorship, which are kept or shared depending on each host's agreement.
- Hosting fees. Cities and organisers pay to stage events. In Taiyuan in 2023, a hosting fee of about RMB5m was paid out of public money.
- Investment. An outside investor took a 15% stake in WTT, and the ITTF sold a further 10% for US$12.1m, according to the 2025 accounts.

The accounts do not give a standalone figure for each stream. They report revenue in a small number of lines, and the most important of those is commercial rights. Sponsorship, media and hosting rights are grouped together, so it is not possible to see how much of the largest line comes from any single source.
## What the 2025 accounts show

Total income for the group rose from US$61.2m in 2024 to US$71.1m in 2025, an increase of 16%. Total expenses rose from US$59.6m to US$85.5m, an increase of 43%. The result swung from a surplus of US$1.5m to a deficit of US$14.4m. Costs grew nearly three times as fast as income.

The mix changed more than the total. Commercial rights income, the largest line in 2024, fell slightly, from US$41.0m to US$39.7m. Event income, which covers what the group earns from running events, roughly doubled, from US$11.3m to US$22.8m. Eleven worked out the shares of total revenue: in 2024 commercial rights made up 78% and event income 21%. In 2025 the shares were 63% and 36%.

That shift matters. Event income carries the costs of running tournaments, from venues and broadcast production to staff and player logistics, so the more the group earns from events, the more of their risk it carries. The 2025 accounts show that cost growth outpaced income growth, and that the new event revenue did not cover it.

The group also carries a short-term strain. Current liabilities exceeded current assets by US$20.2m at the end of 2025, up from US$7.3m a year earlier. The auditor draws attention to a "material uncertainty related to going concern" and says its opinion is not modified in respect of that matter. The next year or two will show whether the group can close that gap.
## The stake nobody could see

The sharpest questions are about ownership. The ITTF's 2025 accounts say World Table Tennis Pte Ltd is 85% owned by the group in both 2024 and 2025, which leaves 15% with someone else. The minutes of the ITTF's executive committee from March 2022, as reported by HK01, record a shareholder agreement with World Sports Industry (Beijing) Co Ltd. The reports differ on the terms. HK01 describes two US$3m debt-to-equity conversions and US$12m of ten-year training services. The Mail & Guardian reports about US$9.2m in cash. Neither the ITTF's accounts nor its 2025 statement names the shareholder.

The identity of the investor has been reported but not confirmed. HK01 reports that a 2024 AGM working document prepared by Steve Dainton named Lei Zhenjian, and that the name matches the founder of Leshi Sports, a company that collapsed. It calls him the most likely holder of the 15%, without confirming it. The Mail & Guardian describes Lei as a Chinese businessman who now sits on WTT's board. Liu Guoliang, president of the Chinese Table Tennis Association and chairman of WTT's council since 2020, is named in the same reporting, and neither report says he holds the stake.

The timetable is part of the problem. The ITTF's 2025 statement says the release of the 2023 accounts "took longer than anticipated", and attributes the delay to restructuring "value-in-kind agreements with WTT investors", reclassifying assets and changing auditors. The federation's website had said the 2023 report would be released in the first half of 2024. As of January 2025, according to HK01, it had not appeared.

The Mail & Guardian published the most detailed account we found in September 2026. It reports allegations and questions about control, the valuation of the debt conversion and whether revenue reaches the 227 member associations. It reports the ITTF's response: the federation said the material contains serious assertions about named individuals that have not been substantiated, engaged PwC for an external review and set up a taskforce. The article itself says none of its questions individually establishes criminal conduct. The review is not yet finished, so there is no finding either way.
## Tournaments and their losses

Tournament-level figures are scarce, and the accounts do not provide them. Eleven found three reference points. The first is Taiyuan in 2023, which made a loss despite about RMB8.15m of public money, as set out in part one. The second is the China Smash, where the organisers announced close to RMB60m of box office in 2024. The third is the US Smash. The South China Morning Post reported in June 2026 that many opening-day tickets were unsold, and attributed an eight-figure deficit in the 2025 accounts to WTT. The statements read for this piece record the loss for the group as a whole and do not name the US Smash or WTT, so that attribution is the newspaper's.

This pattern is common in sport. A host can accept a loss for publicity, tourism and prestige, and the event owner can still earn fees. Whether the arrangement works for WTT depends on how much of each event's income it keeps, and on the cost of the venue, production and travel that it takes on. That is exactly the detail the published accounts leave out, and it is the one thing Eleven would most like to see.
## Where the next money might come from

WTT is looking at India. Ultimate Table Tennis (UTT) has a three-year domestic broadcast deal with JioStar running to 2027, and UTT reported 20 million viewers across TV and streaming in 2024, a 1.3-times increase on the year before. A SportBusiness report describes WTT setting up a majority-owned Indian company, WTT Event Management India, at a cost of between US$3m and US$5m, with talks with UTT's chair, Vita Dani, about outside investment. Dainton said: "We have a big job to do, not only in broadcast, but in sponsorship, and in general awareness."

That is a bet on a market with a large audience and little commercial history, and it will cost money before it earns any. It is also a test of the model: if WTT can turn India's domestic audience into sponsorship and media revenue, the group's costs may be covered. If not, the India venture will add to the expansion costs that the 2025 accounts already show rising.
## Is it sustainable?

The case for WTT is real, and the federation makes it clearly. Commercial and events revenue grew from US$16m in 2019 to more than US$52m in 2024. Prize money rose from US$5.3m to more than US$10m over the same period, according to Dainton's presentation to the 2024 AGM. WTT made its first profit in 2024, and the ITTF says its reserve remains stable at US$6.8m.

The case against rests on the 2025 result and on how the money is structured. Costs rose much faster than income. Event income has grown, so the group carries more of the cost of running events itself. Current liabilities exceed current assets. The ownership of 15% of WTT has never been fully explained in the ITTF's published documents. And revenue is not split by market, so the central question of how much depends on China cannot be answered.

China Daily reported Dainton's view that newer markets typically need two to three years to mature commercially. The 2025 accounts suggest the group is paying for that maturing period now, and the next set of accounts will show whether the expansion is paying back.

Eleven's verdict is that the model has not yet been proven. The 2024 profit shows it can make money in a good year. The 2025 accounts show what it costs to grow. Three things would settle the question: a set of WTT-level accounts, a breakdown of revenue by market, and the outcome of the PwC review together with the 2026 figures.
Until the accounts are split by market and by event, the answer to who pays for table tennis will remain partly a matter of trust.
